When you do something quantitatively, you are dealing with it through numbers, amounts, or measurements — not through feelings, opinions, or descriptions.

Think of it this way: the word lives inside the idea of quantity (how much, how many, how large). So to approach something quantitatively means to put a number on it, count it, measure it, or express it in a way that can be calculated.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Example

Imagine your friend asks: "How was the party?"

You could answer in two ways:

Way 1 (NOT quantitatively):
"It was lively, fun, and a bit overwhelming."
→ This uses feelings and descriptions. There is no number here.

Way 2 (Quantitatively):
"There were 47 people, the music was at 85 decibels, and it lasted 4 hours."
→ This uses numbers and measurable facts. This is the quantitative way.

So when someone says they are measuring or describing something quantitatively, they mean they are expressing it in a form that can be counted, calculated, or compared using actual numbers.

Whenever you see or use the word quantitatively, it is always answering questions like:

  • How much?
  • How many?
  • By how much?
  • To what degree (in numbers)?

For example:

  • "The new drug quantitatively reduced pain by 60%." → By exactly how much? 60%.
  • "The two cities differ quantitatively in population." → Their difference is expressed as a number, not just "one is bigger."
  • "The students improved quantitatively on their test scores." → The improvement is shown through actual score numbers, not just "they got better."

To truly lock in the meaning of quantitatively, it helps to know its opposite: qualitatively.

  • Qualitatively = describing the nature, quality, or character of something → using words, feelings, or categories.
  • Quantitatively = describing the amount, size, or degree of something → using numbers and measurements.

Example:

A doctor examines a patient's recovery.

  • Qualitatively, the patient feels much better, looks healthier, and seems more energetic. (Words and observations.)
  • Quantitatively, the patient's blood pressure dropped from 160 to 120, heart rate normalized to 72 bpm, and inflammation markers fell by 40%. (Numbers and measurements.)

Both are valid ways to look at the same thing — but they are fundamentally different approaches. Quantitatively is always the numbers-and-measurement path.
Where You Will Commonly Encounter This Word

This word appears most often when someone wants to be precise and objective, especially in:

Science and research: "The experiment quantitatively measured the rate of chemical reactions." — Scientists are not guessing; they are recording exact numbers.

Business and finance: "The company quantitatively assessed its losses at $3.2 million." — The loss isn't described as "huge" or "bad"; it is pinned to an exact figure.

Everyday comparisons: "Team A quantitatively outperformed Team B — scoring 95 goals versus 61." — The performance isn't just opinion; it's backed by scoreline numbers.

Health and fitness: "She quantitatively tracked her calorie intake every day." — She counted exact numbers, not just ate "less."
An Important Nuance: Comparisons and Changes

Quantitatively is especially powerful when comparing two things or tracking change over time, because numbers make comparisons undeniably clear.

  • "Product A is quantitatively superior — it lasts 3,000 hours versus Product B's 1,200 hours."
  • "Crime in the city has quantitatively decreased — from 4,800 incidents last year to 3,100 this year."

In both cases, without the numbers, you'd just have an opinion ("Product A is better" or "crime went down"). With the numbers, the statement becomes a measurable, verifiable fact. That is precisely the power of doing something quantitatively.
The Subtle Shade of Meaning: Objectivity and Rigor

There is also a subtle professional tone to the word. When someone says they are approaching something quantitatively, they are also signalling:

  • "I am being rigorous and precise."
  • "I am not relying on gut feeling or vague impressions."
  • "My conclusions can be checked, repeated, and verified by others."

This is why scientists, economists, researchers, and analysts love this word. It signals that their work is grounded in measurable evidence, not guesswork.

Quantitatively = in terms of numbers, amounts, or measurable data — not feelings or descriptions.

Any time you see this word, ask yourself: "Is someone using actual numbers or measurements here?" If yes, that is quantitatively at work.
